question: On 6 June 2025, the Attica Region (Greece) adopted decision 864/20251 to redevelop the Prosfygika district in Athens using National Strategic Reference Framework (NSRF) funds, with the Commission allocating European Regional Development Fund/European Social Fund Plus (ERDF/ESF+) resources2.

Without consulting the residents, official documents falsely classify the inhabited complex of Prosfygika as ‘vacant’, circumventing Article 8 of Regulation (EU)2021/10603. Prosfygika is a vibrant community of 400 people, including 50 minors and vulnerable groups, yet EU social inclusion funds are being used to dismantle an existing social housing model via forced evictions45.

This threat triggered protests, an international solidarity network, and two hunger strikes – one exceeding 120 days6 - jeopardising lives. Greece has no national social housing framework, yet the project designates the renovated buildings as social housing – failing to comply with enabling condition 4.4 (Annex IV, Regulation (EU)2021/1060). 1.
Was the Commission informed that the complex is inhabited, and does it consider the ‘vacant’ classification a violation of Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2021/1060?
Will the Commission suspend reimbursement under Article 15(6) until Greece’s compliance with enabling condition 4.4 is ensured and civil society participation is guaranteed?

answer: 1. In February 2026, the Commission approved the mid-term review of the Attica 2021-2027 Programme. This includes, under the European Regional Development Fund specific objective 4.

7 ‘Promoting access to affordable and sustainable housing’, an action aiming to support the restoration and energy-efficient renovation of a housing complex on Alexandra Avenue in Athens, owned by the Region, to make it available primarily to vulnerable groups. Prior to Commission’s approval, the programme amendment was approved by the monitoring committee, including the partners (1). 2.
The thematic enabling condition 4.4 is not applicable to the above action which falls under the specific objective 4.7 (2).

3. Cohesion policy is under shared management; therefore, Member States are responsible for selecting projects and overseeing their implementation. Throughout the design and implementation of support, including the selection of operations, horizontal principles (3), including the respect for fundamental principles under the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, must be respected.

Member States are also required to have mechanisms (4) in place to ensure compliance with the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU (5). The proposed Council Recommendation on fighting housing exclusion (6) emphasises long-term person-centred solutions and prevention to housing exclusion and homelessness.

It highlights the need for development of mitigation measures and cooperation mechanisms to reduce eviction and homelessness risks. The European Convention on Human Rights and the European Social Charter (7) require legal protection for those facing eviction. This includes also consulting affected parties for alternative solutions and guaranteeing dignified, alternative accommodation when evictions occur.
In accordance with Article 8 of the Common Provisions Regulation (CPR) (EU) 2021/1060: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?
